mainTopic: The cruelty of סדום, then the מרגלים and עדת קרח and their share in עולם הבא
overview: This amud finishes the stories about the cruelty of סדום. An orphan turns their unfair herding rule against them. The גמרא then lists more of their twisted laws, names their four corrupt judges, and shows how a beaten launderer is ordered to pay his attacker. אליעזר עבד אברהם beats their system three times: with the judge, with the bed, and at the wedding. The worst story is a young woman killed for secretly feeding the poor, and רב reads the 'great cry' of סדום as being about her. The גמרא then returns to the משנה: the מרגלים have no share in עולם הבא, and תנאים argue about whether עדת קרח does. Finally, the גמרא reads the names in the פסוק about קרח and his partners as hints, and begins רב's story of how און בן פלת's wife saved him. That story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The orphan's ruling on the hides
steps.stepSummary: The orphan announces how the hides of the oxen should be split: owners of one ox get one hide, people with no ox get two.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whoever has an ox takes one hide, and whoever has no ox takes two hides.
steps.whatsHappening: The story from earlier continues: the orphan who was given everyone's oxen to herd killed them, and now he announces how to divide the hides. Strangely, people with no ox get more.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sounds absurd, and it is meant to. The orphan is copying the 'logic' of a rule אנשי סדום made earlier. The next steps show how he turns their own system against them.

phrases.english: One who has an ox –
let him take one hide,
one who does not have an ox –
let him take two hides.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִית לֵיהּ תּוֹרָא – נִשְׁקוֹל חַד מַשְׁכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the orphan story from before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Owners of an ox get one hide; non-owners get two.

steps.title: The people ask what this means
steps.stepSummary: אנשי סדום ask the orphan why he is dividing the hides this way.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: What is this?
steps.whatsHappening: The people protest and ask for the reason behind his strange division. This sets up the orphan's clever answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their question shows they think his rule is unfair. That is exactly the point, because they don't notice that their own rule was just as unfair.

keyTerms.meaning: what is this? (asking for the reason)

phrases.english: They said to him: What is this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the ruling in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason for giving non-owners more hides than owners.

steps.title: The end matches the beginning
steps.stepSummary: The orphan explains that his rule mirrors their herding rule: whoever had no ox herded twice as long, so now he gets twice the hides.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: The end of the rule follows the start of the rule. At the start, an ox-owner herded for one day and a non-owner herded for two days. So at the end, an ox-owner takes one hide and a non-owner takes two.
steps.whatsHappening: The orphan answers by pointing to their own law. They made poor people with no oxen do double the herding work, so he gives them double the hides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The original rule was cruel: people with nothing to gain had to do more work. The orphan follows the same pattern to the end, so the people of סדום get a taste of their own unfairness.
steps.whatToRemember: The orphan defeated סדום by using their own twisted 'fairness' against them.

phrases.english: He said to them:
The end of the rule is like the start of the rule.
What was the start of the rule?

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִית לֵיהּ תּוֹרָא – מַרְעֵי חַד יוֹמָא,
phrases.english: One who has an ox herds for one day,

phrases.aramaic: דְּלֵית לֵיהּ תּוֹרֵי – מַרְעֵי תְּרֵי יוֹמֵי.
phrases.english: one who has no oxen herds for two days.
So too the end of the rule:

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִית לֵיהּ חַד תּוֹרָא – לִשְׁקוֹל חַד,
phrases.english: one who has one ox takes one,
one who has no ox takes two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The division of hides mirrors their own rule that non-owners herd twice as long.

steps.title: The ferry fee rule
steps.stepSummary: Another סדום rule: crossing on the ferry costs one זוז, and not using the ferry costs two.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who crosses on a ferry pays one זוז; one who does not cross on the ferry pays two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lists another unfair law of סדום. Someone who avoids the ferry and wades through the water still pays, and pays double.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule punishes a person for not using a service. It is the same upside-down pattern as the herding rule: the less you get, the more you pay.

phrases.english: One who crosses on a ferry – let him give one zuz,
one who does not cross on the ferry – let him give two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new example of סדום's unfair laws.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Using the ferry costs one זוז; not using it costs two.

steps.title: Stealing one piece at a time
steps.stepSummary: When someone had bricks or drying garlic or onions, each person took just one piece and claimed it was only one.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone had a row of bricks, each person would come and take one and say, 'I only took one.' If someone spread out garlic or onions, each person would come, take one, and say, 'I only took one.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא describes how אנשי סדום stole together. Each person took one tiny item, so no single person seemed to be stealing anything worth complaining about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each person's excuse is 'just one piece', but together they wipe out the owner's whole supply. It is cruelty hidden behind a claim that each act was too small to matter.

phrases.english: One who had a row of bricks,

phrases.aramaic: אָתֵי כֹּל חַד וְחַד שָׁקֵיל חֲדָא,
phrases.english: each and every one would come and take one,
and say to him: I only took one.
One who would spread out garlic or onions,

phrases.aramaic: אֲתוֹ כֹּל חַד וְחַד שָׁקֵיל חֲדָא,
phrases.english: each and every one would come and take one,
and say to him: I only took one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of סדום's wicked practices.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Group theft disguised as taking 'only one' each.

steps.title: The four judges of סדום
steps.stepSummary: סדום had four judges, and their names describe their lying and corruption.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were four judges in סדום: שקראי, שקרוראי, זייפי, and מצלי דינא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces the judges of סדום. This sets up the next step, which shows the kind of rulings they gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their names mean 'liar', 'big liar', 'forger', and 'twister of justice'. The court itself was meant to cover up wrongdoing, not stop it.

phrases.english: There were four judges in Sodom,
Shakrai and Shakrurai,
phrases.notes: These names come from שקר, a lie: 'liar' and 'big liar'.

phrases.english: Zayfai and Matzlei Dina.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the town's laws to its judges.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: סדום's four judges were named for lying and corruption.

steps.title: The judges' twisted rulings
steps.stepSummary: Three examples of absurd rulings: the attacker gets the wife, the attacker gets the donkey, and the victim pays the attacker.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone struck another man's wife and she miscarried, they told the husband: Give her to him so he can make her pregnant for you. If someone cut off the ear of another's donkey, they told the owner: Give it to him until the ear grows back. If someone wounded another person, they told the victim: Pay him a fee, since he let your blood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives examples of how the judges ruled. Each time, the victim ends up giving something to the person who hurt him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each ruling pretends to 'fix' the damage, but it rewards the attacker instead. The wounding case treats the injury like a paid medical bloodletting, so the victim owes money.
steps.confusionAlert: In all three cases the victim pays or hands something over. That is the whole point: the court of סדום turned justice upside down.

phrases.english: One who struck his friend's wife
and she miscarried,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some leave it out. The meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: they would say to [the husband]: Give her to him
so that he will make her pregnant for you.
One who cut off the ear of his friend's donkey,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: הֲבַהּ נִיהֲלֵיהּ עַד דְּקָדְחָא.
phrases.english: they said to [the owner]: Give it to him until it grows back.
One who wounded his friend,
they would say to [the victim]: Give him a fee
since he let your blood.
phrases.notes: Letting blood was a medical treatment people paid for, so the judges pretend the wound was a 'treatment'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the rulings of the judges introduced in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The judges of סדום made the victim compensate the attacker.

steps.title: The raised river-crossing fee
steps.stepSummary: A version of the ferry law: four זוזים for the ferry, eight for crossing through the water.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who crossed on a ferry paid four זוזים; one who crossed through the water paid eight זוזים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the ferry rule again, this time with higher prices. This sets up the story of the launderer that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Again, the person who uses no service pays double. Here the rule is the background for a real case that shows how the law and the courts worked together.

phrases.english: One who crossed on a ferry gives four zuz,
one who crossed through the water gives eight zuz.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restates the ferry law to set up a story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Ferry costs four, wading costs eight.

steps.title: The launderer is charged and beaten
steps.stepSummary: A launderer arrives and is charged four זוזים. He says he walked through the water, so they demand eight. He refuses, and they wound him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once a launderer arrived there. They told him: Pay four זוזים. He said: I crossed through the water. They said: If so, pay eight, since you crossed through the water. He did not pay, and they wounded him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that puts the ferry law into action. The launderer tries to avoid the ferry fee and ends up owing more, and he gets beaten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His excuse makes things worse under their law, which shows how the system trapped everyone. His refusal leads to violence, which sets up the court case.

phrases.english: One time a certain launderer came,
he happened to arrive there.
They said to him: Give four zuz.
He said to them: I crossed through the water.
They said to him: If so,
give eight, since you crossed through the water.
He did not give. They wounded him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the law of step 8 to a story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The launderer is charged double, refuses, and is wounded.

steps.title: The judge makes the victim pay twice
steps.stepSummary: The launderer goes to court. The judge orders him to pay his attacker for 'letting his blood' and also to pay the eight זוזים.
steps.simpleTranslation: He came before the judge. The judge said to him: Pay him a fee because he let your blood, and pay eight זוזים because you crossed through the water.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends in court. Instead of helping the victim, the דיין makes him pay twice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The judge applies the 'bloodletting fee' ruling from step 7 together with the ferry law from step 8. The victim walks in hurt and leaves owing even more, which shows how deep the corruption in סדום went.
steps.whatToRemember: In סדום, the laws and the courts worked together to rob the weak and reward the attacker.
steps.whyThisMatters: These stories show that the evil of סדום was not lawlessness. It was cruelty dressed up as law and justice.

phrases.english: He came before the judge.
He said to him: Give him a fee
since he let your blood,
and eight zuz since you crossed through the water.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the launderer story with the judge's ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The judge of סדום combined both unjust rules, so the victim had to pay his attacker and also pay the doubled crossing fee.

steps.title: אליעזר is wounded and the judge orders him to pay
steps.stepSummary: אליעזר עבד אברהם comes to סדום, is wounded, and the judge tells him to pay his attacker for 'letting his blood.'
steps.simpleTranslation: אליעזר, אברהם's servant, happened to come to סדום, and they wounded him. He went to the judge, who told him: Pay your attacker a fee, because he let your blood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new story in which אליעזר meets the same crooked ruling we just saw. This step sets up his clever reply in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same twisted law as in step 10: the victim pays the attacker as if the attacker were a paid bloodletter. Now a wise visitor faces it, so we expect him to find a way out.

phrases.aramaic: אֱלִיעֶזֶר עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אִיתְרְמִי הָתָם, פַּדְיוּהּי.
phrases.english: Eliezer, servant of Abraham, happened to come there, and they wounded him.
He came before the judge.
The judge said to him: Give him a fee,
since he let your blood.
phrases.notes: Bloodletting was a paid treatment back then, so the judge pretends the attacker did him a medical favor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same absurd 'pay for bloodletting' ruling from step 10 to אליעזר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The judge of סדום orders the wounded אליעזר to pay his attacker.

steps.title: אליעזר wounds the judge and turns the ruling around
steps.stepSummary: אליעזר wounds the judge and tells him to pay the fee he now owes directly to the attacker, so אליעזר keeps his own money.
steps.simpleTranslation: אליעזר took a stone and wounded the judge. The judge said: What is this? אליעזר answered: The fee you now owe me, give it to that man, and my money stays where it is.
steps.whatsHappening: אליעזר uses the judge's own rule against him. This ends the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If wounding someone earns a fee, then the judge now owes אליעזר a fee. אליעזר simply passes that debt on to his attacker, so he never pays anything himself.
steps.whatToRemember: אליעזר beats סדום's twisted law by using it exactly as they wrote it, so the judge ends up paying.

phrases.english: He took a stone and wounded the judge.
The judge said: What is this?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַגְרָא דִּנְפַק לִי מִינָּךְ,
phrases.english: He said to him: The fee that is coming to me from you,
give it to that man,
phrases.notes: He means the man who wounded him in the first place.

phrases.english: and my money will stay where it is.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives אליעזר's clever response to the judge's ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The judge's own logic forces him to pay, and אליעזר pays nothing.

steps.title: The beds of סדום that cut or stretched guests
steps.stepSummary: סדום had beds for guests; a guest too long was cut, and a guest too short was stretched.
steps.simpleTranslation: They had beds that they would put guests on. If a guest was longer than the bed, they cut him. If he was shorter, they stretched him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new example of סדום's cruelty to guests. It sets up the next story about אליעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bed looks like hospitality, but it is really a way to hurt anyone who visits. Nobody fits exactly, so every guest gets hurt.

phrases.english: They had beds
on which they would lay guests.
When he was longer, they would cut him;
when he was shorter, they would stretch him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new example of סדום's wickedness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Guests in סדום were cut or stretched to fit the bed.

steps.title: אליעזר escapes the bed with a vow
steps.stepSummary: When told to lie on the bed, אליעזר says he vowed not to lie on a bed since his mother died.
steps.simpleTranslation: אליעזר came there. They told him: Get up and lie on the bed. He said: I made a vow that since the day my mother died, I do not lie on a bed.
steps.whatsHappening: אליעזר meets the deadly bed and avoids it. This closes the bed story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not fight them openly. He uses a vow, which they cannot easily argue with, as a polite way to refuse.

phrases.english: Eliezer, servant of Abraham, happened to come there.
They said to him: Get up, lie on the bed.
He said to them: I made a vow
that since the day my mother died
I do not lie on a bed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how אליעזר escaped the beds described in step 13.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: אליעזר avoids the bed by saying he is bound by a vow.

steps.title: Fake charity that starved the poor
steps.stepSummary: The people gave a poor visitor marked coins but refused to sell him bread, then took their coins back after he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: When a poor man came to them, each person gave him a dinar with his own name written on it. But they would not give him bread. When he died, each person came and took back his own coin.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another example of סדום's cruelty, this time against the poor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The giving looks generous, but since nobody would sell him food, the coins were useless. Writing their names on the coins let each person reclaim his money after the poor man starved.

phrases.english: When a poor person would happen to come to them,

phrases.aramaic: יְהַבוּ לֵיהּ כֹּל חַד וְחַד דִּינָרָא,
phrases.english: each and every one would give him a dinar,
with his name written on it.
phrases.notes: The giver's name, not the poor man's, so each person could find his own coin later.

phrases.english: But they would not hand him bread.
When he would die,

phrases.aramaic: אָתֵי כֹּל חַד וְחַד שָׁקֵיל דִּידֵיהּ.
phrases.english: each and every one would come and take his own.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, separate example of סדום's wickedness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: סדום gave the poor charity that was impossible to use, then took it back after they died.

steps.title: The wedding rule: whoever invites a guest loses his cloak
steps.stepSummary: סדום agreed that anyone who invites a man to a wedding has his cloak taken.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what they agreed among themselves: Anyone who invites a man to a wedding will have his cloak taken off.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states another law of סדום. This is a setup for the wedding story in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule punishes hospitality itself, so nobody would dare invite outsiders. אליעזר will use this rule against them.

phrases.english: This is what they agreed among themselves:

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל מַאן דְּמַזְמֵין גַּבְרָא לְבֵי הִילּוּלָא,
phrases.english: Whoever invites a man to a wedding feast,
his cloak will be stripped off.
phrases.notes: It is the inviter who loses his cloak, not the guest.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a new law of סדום that sets up the next story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In סדום, the punishment for inviting a guest to a wedding was losing one's cloak.

steps.title: אליעזר arrives at the wedding and is challenged
steps.stepSummary: אליעזר comes to a wedding, gets no bread, sits at the end, and is asked who invited him.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a wedding, and אליעזר came there, but they gave him no bread. When he wanted to eat, אליעזר came and sat at the very end behind everyone. They asked him: Who invited you here?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets the scene at the wedding. This step prepares for אליעזר's trick in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question 'who invited you' is dangerous because of the rule in step 16. Whoever is named as the inviter will lose his cloak.

phrases.english: There was this wedding feast,
Eliezer happened to come there,
and they did not give him bread.
When he wanted to eat,
Eliezer came and sat at the end, behind all of them.
They said to him: Who invited you here?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Puts the wedding rule from step 16 into a story with אליעזר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אליעזר is at the wedding and must say who invited him.

steps.title: אליעזר chases out every guest and eats the meal
steps.stepSummary: אליעזר tells each neighbor 'you invited me'; each one flees to save his cloak, and אליעזר eats the whole meal.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to the man sitting next to him: You invited me. That man thought: Maybe they will hear that I invited him and strip my clothes. So he took his cloak and ran outside. אליעזר did this to all of them until they all left, and he ate the meal.
steps.whatsHappening: אליעזר uses the wedding rule against the guests themselves. This closes the story and the section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each guest is afraid of the very rule סדום made, so he runs away instead of arguing. In the end the people who would not share a single piece of bread lose the entire feast to אליעזר.
steps.whatToRemember: In all these stories, אליעזר defeats סדום by turning their own cruel rules against them.

phrases.english: He said to the one sitting next to him: You invited me.
That man said to himself: Perhaps they will hear about me that I invited him,
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are the corrected wording; they tell us what the man was thinking.

phrases.english: and they will strip the clothes of this man.
phrases.notes: 'This man' is his polite way of talking about himself.

phrases.english: The one sitting next to him took his cloak
and ran outside.
And he did the same to all of them
until they all went out,
and he ate the meal himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ לְהָהוּא דְּיָתֵיב: אַתְּ זַמֵּנְתַּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives אליעזר's answer to the question asked in step 17.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The wedding rule backfires, every guest flees, and אליעזר eats the whole meal.

steps.title: The young woman who secretly fed the poor
steps.stepSummary: A young woman hid bread in a jug to feed the poor. When she was found out, the people of סדום smeared her with honey and left her on the wall, where hornets ate her.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a young woman who used to bring bread to the poor hidden in a water jug. When it was discovered, they smeared her with honey and stood her on top of the city wall. Hornets came and ate her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells one more story about the cruelty of סדום. This is the worst one in the series.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier stories showed סדום's laws against kindness to guests and the poor. Here the cruelty reaches its peak: a person is killed just for feeding the hungry. This story sets up the next step, which links it to a פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: the matter was revealed, it came out

phrases.english: There was a certain young woman
who used to take out bread
to the poor in a water jug.
The matter came out;
they smeared her with honey,
and stood her on top of the wall.
Hornets came and ate her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the final and harshest story in the series about סדום's cruelty.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: סדום went as far as killing a girl for secretly feeding the poor.

steps.title: The cry of סדום was over the young woman
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says the cry of סדום 'is great' (רבה). רב יהודה in the name of רב reads this word as hinting to the girl (ריבה). Her death is what sealed סדום's fate.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what is written: 'And ה׳ said: the cry of סדום and עמורה is great (רבה).' רב יהודה said in the name of רב: it is about the matter of the girl (ריבה).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ties the story of the young woman to a פסוק. This closes the whole section about סדום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word רבה ('great') sounds like ריבה ('girl'). רב uses this to say the 'cry' ה׳ heard was really about this girl. So her murder was the last straw that brought the destruction of סדום.

keyTerms.meaning: and this is what is written

steps.whatToRemember: The sin that sealed סדום's fate was killing a girl for her kindness. רב finds it hinted in the word רבה.

phrases.english: And this is what is written:
"And ה׳ said: the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah
phrases.notes: בראשית 18:20

phrases.english: is great."
And Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
It was about the matter of the girl.
phrases.notes: רבה ('great') sounds like ריבה ('girl'), so רב hears the word as pointing to her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connects the story of the young woman to a פסוק and closes the סדום section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The 'great cry' of סדום refers to the murdered girl, and her death sealed their judgment.

steps.title: The מרגלים have no share in עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the משנה. It teaches that the מרגלים have no share in עולם הבא, and it splits a פסוק in two to prove it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The מרגלים have no share in עולם הבא, as it says: 'And the men who brought out an evil report of the land died by the plague.' 'And they died' means in this world; 'by the plague' means for עולם הבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now leaves סדום and returns to the list in the משנה. The next group is the מרגלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק seems to say the same thing twice: they died, and they died by plague. The extra words are read as two separate punishments. 'They died' is their death in this world, and 'by the plague' is losing עולם הבא.

keyTerms.meaning: the spies sent by משה to the land
a share in the World to Come
a bad report about the land

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'they died by the plague' as one event. The גמרא splits it on purpose: half is about this world and half is about עולם הבא.

phrases.english: The spies have no share
in the World to Come,
as it says: "And the men died,
those who brought out an evil report of the land,
by the plague."
phrases.notes: במדבר 14:37

phrases.english: "And they died" means in this world;
"by the plague" means for the World to Come.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְרַגְּלִים אֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the סדום stories and goes back to the next group listed in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מרגלים lose both this world and עולם הבא, based on the two parts of the פסוק.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: עדת קרח has no share in עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא says עדת קרח has no share in עולם הבא. He splits the פסוק in two: 'the earth covered them' is this world, and 'they were lost from among the congregation' is עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: עדת קרח has no share in עולם הבא, as it says: 'And the earth covered them' (in this world), 'and they were lost from among the congregation' (for עולם הבא). These are the words of רבי עקיבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves to the next group, עדת קרח. רבי עקיבא gives his view that they have no share.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This uses the same method as the מרגלים: one פסוק, two phrases, two punishments. Being swallowed by the earth is their death here. Being 'lost' means they are cut off from עולם הבא too.

keyTerms.meaning: the group that rebelled with קרח
and they were lost, they perished

phrases.aramaic: עֲדַת קֹרַח אֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
phrases.english: The assembly of Korach has no share in the World to Come,
as it says: "And the earth covered them"
phrases.notes: במדבר 16:33

phrases.english: meaning in this world;
"and they were lost from among the congregation"
meaning for the World to Come.
These are the words of Rabbi Akiva.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲדַת קֹרַח אֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same split-the-פסוק method as the מרגלים, now for עדת קרח.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי עקיבא: עדת קרח has no share in עולם הבא.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר‎: ה׳ brings down and raises up
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר disagrees with רבי עקיבא. He applies the פסוק‎ 'ה׳ kills and brings to life, brings down to the grave and raises up' to עדת קרח, meaning they will rise again.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: about them the verse says, 'ה׳ kills and brings to life; He brings down to the grave and raises up.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion in the משנה argues with רבי עקיבא. רבי אליעזר holds that עדת קרח does have hope.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עדת קרח went down into the ground alive. רבי אליעזר reads the פסוק about ה׳ 'bringing down and raising up' as speaking about them. So they went down, but they will come back up and have a share in עולם הבא.
steps.whatToRemember: There is a real argument about עדת קרח. רבי עקיבא says they have no share, and רבי אליעזר says they will rise again.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says:
About them the verse says:
"ה׳ kills and brings to life,
He brings down to the grave and raises up."
phrases.notes: שמואל א 2:6

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to רבי עקיבא within the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אליעזר: עדת קרח will be raised up and does have a share in עולם הבא.

steps.title: A ברייתא repeats רבי עקיבא's view on עדת קרח
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches the same words of רבי עקיבא as the משנה. This repetition sets up a different person who disagrees with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Our רבנן taught: עדת קרח has no share in עולם הבא, as it says: 'And the earth covered them' (in this world), 'and they were lost from among the congregation' (for עולם הבא). These are the words of רבי עקיבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that repeats רבי עקיבא's view word for word. It is setting up a new opinion that comes right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is said about רבי עקיבא here. The point of quoting the ברייתא is that it names a different person arguing with him, and that comes in the next step.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a copying mistake. The ברייתא repeats רבי עקיבא's words because it pairs them with a different person who disagrees.

phrases.english: Our Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: עֲדַת קֹרַח אֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
phrases.english: The assembly of Korach has no share in the World to Come,
as it says: "And the earth covered them"
meaning in this world;
"and they were lost from among the congregation"
meaning for the World to Come.
These are the words of Rabbi Akiva.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא with the same words of רבי עקיבא, as the setup for a different opposing view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא confirms רבי עקיבא's view as stated in the משנה.

steps.title: רבי יהודה בן בתירא: Like a lost object that is searched for
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן בתירא disagrees with רבי עקיבא. He says עדת קרח is like a lost object that someone searches for and finds, using the פסוק 'I have strayed like a lost sheep; seek out Your servant.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה בן בתירא says: they are like a lost object that is searched for, as it says: 'I have strayed like a lost sheep; seek out Your servant, for I have not forgotten Your מצוות.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a different opinion against רבי עקיבא. רבי יהודה בן בתירא sees עדת קרח as lost but not gone forever.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא read 'they were lost' (ויאבדו) as being cut off for good. רבי יהודה בן בתירא reads 'lost' like a lost sheep that its owner goes looking for. Something lost is still sought and can be found, so עדת קרח still has hope.

keyTerms.meaning: a lost object that is searched for

steps.whatToRemember: Against רבי עקיבא, two תנאים give עדת קרח hope: רבי אליעזר ('He brings down and raises up') and רבי יהודה בן בתירא ('like a lost object that is searched for').
steps.whyThisMatters: The same word, 'lost', is read in two opposite ways. רבי עקיבא hears it as gone forever, and רבי יהודה בן בתירא hears it as waiting to be found.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says:
They are like a lost object that is searched for,
as it says: "I have strayed like a lost sheep;
seek out Your servant,
for I have not forgotten Your מצוות."
phrases.notes: תהלים 119:176

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ברייתא's opposing view to the repeated words of רבי עקיבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה בן בתירא: עדת קרח is 'lost' like something that will be searched for and found, so they are not cut off forever.

steps.title: ריש לקיש reads קרח's family names as hints
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש explains every word in 'ויקח קרח בן יצהר בן קהת בן לוי' as a hint to קרח's bad end.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And קרח took': ריש לקיש says he took a bad deal for himself. 'קרח' means a bald spot, a gap, was made in ישראל because of him. 'Son of יצהר' means he made the whole world boil against him like the midday heat. 'Son of קהת' means he made his parents' teeth go dull. 'Son of לוי' means he became an escort into גיהנם.
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the גמרא has discussed עדת קרח, it goes back to the פסוק that starts the story. ריש לקיש reads each word of it as a hint to קרח's sin and punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every name gets a wordplay. ויקח sounds like מקח, a purchase. קרח sounds like קרחה, a bald spot. יצהר sounds like צהרים, midday. קהת sounds like הקהה, to make dull. לוי sounds like לויה, escorting. Together they show that his whole family line is used to point to his downfall.

keyTerms.meaning: A bad purchase or bad deal
A bald spot, a gap left behind
He made something boil, he stirred up anger
Made the teeth dull, meaning he brought shame

phrases.english: "And Korah took":
phrases.notes: במדבר 16:1.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish says:
That he took a bad purchase for himself.
"Korah": because a bald spot was made in Israel.
phrases.notes: A bald spot means a gap: people of ישראל were lost because of him.

phrases.english: "Son of Izhar": a son who made boil against himself
the whole world, like the heat of midday.
"Son of Kohath": a son who dulled the teeth of his parents.
"Son of Levi": a son who became an escort in Gehinnom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the argument about עדת קרח's share in עולם הבא, the גמרא turns to reading the words of קרח's פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each name in קרח's family line hints at his bad choice and his punishment.

steps.title: Why not also read 'son of יעקב'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פסוק stops at לוי and does not also say 'son of יעקב', which could hint that he twisted himself into גיהנם.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let it also list 'son of יעקב', meaning a son who twisted himself into גיהנם?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question about step 26: if the family names are hints, why does the line stop before יעקב? The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name יעקב also fits a bad hint, since it sounds like עקב, twisting. So the missing name looks strange. The גמרא wants a reason why the Torah left it out.

keyTerms.meaning: Then let it count, let it list

phrases.english: Then let it also list "son of Jacob,"
a son who twisted himself into Gehinnom?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the end of ריש לקיש's list of family names.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the פסוק does not continue the family line up to יעקב.

steps.title: יעקב prayed not to be listed with קרח
steps.stepSummary: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק answers that יעקב prayed that his name would not be connected to the מרגלים or to עדת קרח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק says: יעקב asked for mercy for himself, as it says, 'Let my soul not come into their secret plan; let my honor not join their gathering.' 'Let my soul not come into their plan' means the מרגלים. 'Let my honor not join their gathering' means עדת קרח.
steps.whatsHappening: This answers the question from step 27. יעקב's name is missing because he prayed long ago not to be mentioned with קרח's group.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is a פסוק from יעקב's blessings (בראשית 49:6). The גמרא splits it in two: 'their council' is the מרגלים, and 'their assembly' is עדת קרח. Since יעקב asked not to be linked to them, the Torah stops קרח's family line at לוי.

keyTerms.meaning: A secret plan, a private meeting

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר רַב יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak says:
Jacob asked for mercy for himself,
as it is said: "Into their council let my soul not come;
phrases.notes: בראשית 49:6.

phrases.english: to their assembly let my honor not be joined."
"Into their council let my soul not come": these are the spies.

phrases.aramaic: ״בִּקְהָלָם אַל תֵּחַד כְּבֹדִי״ – זֶה עֲדַת קֹרַח.
phrases.english: "To their assembly let my honor not be joined": this is the assembly of Korah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר רַב יִצְחָק יַעֲקֹב בִּיקֵּשׁ רַחֲמִים עַל עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: יעקב prayed that his name would not be linked to the מרגלים or to עדת קרח, so the Torah stops the line at לוי.

steps.title: Reading the names of דתן, אבירם and און
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the names of קרח's partners as hints: דתן and אבירם for their sin, and און בן פלת for how he was saved.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'דתן': he broke God's law. 'אבירם': he made himself strong against doing תשובה. 'און': he sat in mourning. 'פלת': wonders were done for him. 'Son of ראובן': a son who saw and understood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps reading the same פסוק, now explaining the names of the people who joined קרח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דתן sounds like דת, law. אבירם sounds like איבר, to make strong and stubborn. און sounds like אנינות, deep mourning. פלת sounds like פלאות, wonders. ראובן sounds like ראה, saw. The names of דתן and אבירם show their sin, but the names for און show that he regretted it and was saved.
steps.confusionAlert: Not all the names are bad. דתן and אבירם get bad readings, but the readings for און בן פלת are good, because he was saved, as the next steps tell.

phrases.english: "Dathan": because he broke the law of God,
"Abiram": because he made himself stubborn against doing repentance,
"And On": because he sat in mourning,
phrases.notes: He mourned over what he had done, meaning he regretted it.

phrases.english: "Peleth": because wonders were done for him,
"Son of Reuben": a son who saw and understood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes on from קרח's names to the names of his partners in the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דתן and אבירם's names show their stubborn sin; און בן פלת's names show that he regretted it and was saved.

steps.title: רב: און's wife saved him
steps.stepSummary: רב says און בן פלת was saved by his wife, who told him he gains nothing from the fight, since either way he stays a student.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says: און בן פלת's wife saved him. She said to him: What do you get out of this? If this master is the leader, you are the student, and if that master is the leader, you are still the student.
steps.whatsHappening: רב tells a story explaining how און was saved. Here his wife gives her first argument for leaving the rebellion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 29 only said און regretted it. רב adds that it was his wife who got him out. Her point is simple: whether משה leads or קרח leads, און does not move up, so why risk himself?

keyTerms.meaning: What difference does it make to you?

phrases.english: Rav says:
On son of Peleth, his wife saved him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ: מַאי נָפְקָא לָךְ מִינַּהּ?
phrases.english: She said to him: What difference does it make to you?
If this master is the great one, you are the student,
phrases.notes: "This master" is משה.

phrases.english: and if that master is the great one, you are the student.
phrases.notes: "That master" is קרח. Either way און stays a follower.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אוֹן בֶּן פֶּלֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ הִצִּילַתּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how און came to regret and be saved, as hinted in step 29.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: און בן פלת was saved because his wife talked him out of the rebellion.

steps.title: און's oath and his wife's plan
steps.stepSummary: און says he is trapped by an oath. His wife tells him to sit tight, gets him drunk, puts him to bed inside, and sits at the door.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: What can I do? I was in the meeting and swore to be with them. She said to him: I know that the whole group is holy, as it says, 'For the whole congregation, all of them are holy.' She said: Sit, and I will save you. She gave him wine, got him drunk, and laid him down inside. Then she sat at the door,
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. און explains why he feels stuck, and his wife starts her plan to keep him home. The story goes on in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: און's problem is not that he agrees with קרח, but that he took an oath. His wife quotes קרח's own words, 'all the congregation is holy', and uses that to plan her rescue. She makes sure he cannot leave, then sits at the door; what she does there comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: A plan, a meeting where a plan was made
I swore, I took an oath

phrases.english: He said to her: What shall I do?
I was in the plan, and I swore to be with them.
She said to him: I know
that the whole congregation are holy people,
as it is written: "For the whole congregation, all of them are holy."
phrases.notes: במדבר 16:3. These are קרח's own words against משה.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ: תּוּב, דַּאֲנָא מַצֵּילְנָא לָךְ.
phrases.english: She said to him: Sit, for I will save you.
She gave him wine to drink and made him drunk
and laid him down inside.
And she sat at the door,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב's story: און answers his wife, and she begins her plan.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: און felt bound by his oath, so his wife made sure he could not go, and began a plan built on the group being holy.
